# What We Built, and What We Learned

## The short version, and why it doesn't tell you much

We built Codescope. It's an AI code reviewer — you paste in a chunk of code, or hand it a GitHub link, and it reads the thing back to you: what's broken, what's dangerous, what's just sloppy, and what's actually fine. It streams the answer back live instead of making you sit there watching a spinner think about its life choices. It's deployed, it's public, it has a repository with real history behind it, it has tests that pass, and it has a CI pipeline that goes green when we push. That's the one-paragraph version, and it's true, but it's also the kind of sentence that could describe a hundred different weekends and a hundred different levels of stress to get there. So this is the longer version — the one with the actual texture in it, because we think the texture is the part worth keeping.

This was our first hackathon. Not our first time writing code, not our first side project, but our first time doing this specific, strange thing where you build something from a blank folder to a live URL with a deadline breathing on your neck the entire time, in public, with people who are going to ask you questions about it afterward. We want to be upfront about that, because it colors everything that follows. A lot of what we learned today wasn't really about code. It was about what it feels like to be under that particular kind of pressure for the first time, and what you do with yourself when it shows up.

## What we actually built

Let's start with the thing itself, because it deserves a real description before we get into how messy the process of making it was.

Codescope takes code — either pasted directly in, or pulled straight from a GitHub file URL — and sends it off to Google's Gemini API with a very specific set of instructions: find the security problems first, then the bugs, then the things that aren't wrong exactly but could be better, then the general good habits the code is or isn't following. It asks for all of that back in a strict structure, not a paragraph of prose, so that we can actually render it as something a person can scan in ten seconds instead of read for ten minutes.

The part we're most attached to, if we're honest, is the streaming. When you hit "Run Scan," you don't wait. You watch it. Text starts arriving almost immediately and keeps arriving, live, while the model is still thinking, and then once it's done, the raw stream resolves into the actual structured report — tabs for security, bugs, improvements, best practices, a little dial showing an overall score, colored meters for readability and maintainability and performance and security. There's something almost theatrical about watching an AI "read" your code in real time instead of just being handed a verdict, and we noticed, more than once during testing, that we ourselves kept wanting to paste in one more snippet just to watch it happen again. If a feature makes its own creators want to keep using it for no reason, that's usually a decent sign.

We didn't build that streaming effect with anything exotic. No WebSockets, no special library. Just a server that re-emits the AI's response chunk by chunk as it receives it, over a plain HTTP connection that never technically closes until the whole thing is done, and a browser on the other end reading that connection's body as a stream instead of waiting for the whole response to land at once. It's the kind of trick that feels like magic when you see it working and feels almost embarrassingly simple once you understand what's actually happening under it. We liked that about it. A lot of impressive-looking things, it turns out, are quietly simple once you stop being intimidated by them.

Security findings get their own separate lane in the report, apart from generic bugs, on purpose. We made that call early, sitting there staring at a first draft that lumped everything into one big undifferentiated list, and someone said something like "if I were a judge, or honestly if I were just a developer, I wouldn't want to hunt for the scary stuff buried in a pile of minor nitpicks." So security got promoted. Every finding in that category, and in the bugs category too, comes with a severity tag and, wherever it makes sense, an actual corrected snippet of code — not just a sentence telling you that something is wrong, but something you could genuinely copy and use.

You can skip the copy-paste step entirely and just hand it a GitHub file link instead, and the server goes and fetches that file itself, so there's no wrestling with browser security restrictions that would otherwise get in the way. Every completed scan gets saved automatically to a small file on the server — deliberately not a real database, because for something running on a single free-tier server for a weekend, a database would have been solving a problem we didn't have yet. And when you're happy with a report, one click turns it into a clean Markdown file you could drop straight into a pull request description.

None of these pieces, on their own, are the kind of thing that wins an award for originality. What we're actually proud of is quieter than that: everything above is genuinely working, live, right now, on a real URL, built by people who can explain exactly why each decision was made — not because it sounded impressive, but because we sat with the alternatives and picked the one that made sense for what this actually was.

## The parts nobody puts in the demo

Here's where we want to slow down, because the polished version of this story would skip straight from "we had an idea" to "and then it worked," and that would be a lie by omission.

We started more ambitious than we needed to, and then had to actually finish something. The very first version of this app was small — paste box, button, result underneath. It worked. We could have stopped. Instead we kept adding: GitHub import, then streaming, then the metrics dashboard, then scan history, then export. Every single one of those additions felt justified in the moment, and honestly, we still think they were the right calls. But looking back at the day as a whole, we noticed a pattern in ourselves that's worth naming honestly: building new things is fun in a way that testing old things isn't, and it is very easy to keep chasing that fun feeling right up until you suddenly don't have any time left for the boring-but-necessary parts. We got away with it this time. We don't think we should count on getting away with it next time.

Then, partway through — and this is the part that still makes us laugh a little, in the specific way you laugh at something that stopped being funny about four minutes into it happening — the exact AI model we'd built the whole backend around simply stopped existing. Not "got slower" or "changed its answers a bit." Gone. 404. Google had renamed the whole SDK package and retired the specific model version we were calling, and our server just refused to start, with an error message that gave us maybe one sentence of explanation and no sympathy at all. We had to stop everything, go figure out what had actually changed, migrate over to a new package with a different way of calling it, a new model name, a slightly different response shape — and do all of that without breaking anything else that was already working, while the clock kept doing the one thing clocks do regardless of how you feel about it.
Anything else for the judges:
CodeScope is an AI-powered code review assistant designed to provide developers with a structured first-pass review of their source code.
Key highlights:
AI-powered analysis for security, bugs, performance, maintainability and readability.
Supports reviewing pasted source code and GitHub-imported files.
Uses a structured review skill with a defined input/output contract.

Why I like this version
It gives the judges four things immediately:
What it is → how it works → proof of engineering → limitations/future work.
And importantly, you're not claiming AI is perfect. That actually gives you a strong answer if a judge asks:
“Can we trust the AI completely?”
You can say:
“No. CodeScope is an assistant, not an authority. It provides structured findings, and the developer remains responsible for validating them.”

What We Built:
Gatekeeper is an AI support-operations decision gate. Rather than deploying autonomous chatbots that risk hallucinations or unauthorized refunds, Gatekeeper runs an automated multi-stage AI pipeline (Analyzer, Writer, Reviewer) that prepares resolutions, verifies them against company policy, and halts at a human approval gate before anything is executed. 

How We Built It:
- Stack: Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Supabase PostgreSQL, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, and Vercel AI SDK (powered by Google Gemini Flash).
- State Machine: Governed by strict state transitions (RECEIVED → ANALYZING → DRAFTED → VERIFIED → AWAITING_APPROVAL → EXECUTED/REJECTED).
- AI Pipeline: Uses structured JSON generation (`generateObject`). The Analyzer classifies category and severity; the Writer drafts customer responses and internal actions; the independent Reviewer checks the draft against policy rules to catch hallucinations and block prompt injection overrides.
- Security & Audit: State transitions are executed server-side via atomic Postgres functions (`apply_transition`), secured with Row Level Security (RLS) and an append-only audit event log.

What We Learned:
- Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Engineering: In operations software, combining deterministic state machines with human approval gates provides the speed of AI with zero risk of bad automation.
- Self-Verification: An independent verification stage is critical to detect prompt injections and policy violations before output reaches human operators.
- Agentic Development: Structuring spec documents, task breakdowns, and strict boundaries allowed us to build, test, and ship a production app in record time.
Anything else for the judges:
Live Applications:
- Operations Dashboard: https://usegatekeeper.vercel.app
- Customer Submission Portal: https://usegatekeeper.vercel.app/portal

Key Highlights:
- Live Interactive Demo: You can submit custom inquiries directly on the Customer Portal (/portal) and watch Gatekeeper ingest, analyze, verify, and pause them for review in real-time.
- Security Shield: Visually detects and defends against customer prompt injections (e.g., text asking to "ignore previous instructions").
- Traceability: Every transition is logged with actor provenance (AI, System, or Human).

Known Issues & What's Next:
- Current demo simulates external email/payment execution; next steps would include real webhooks for Zendesk, Intercom, and Stripe.
- Expand policy checks with RAG/vector retrieval for massive multi-page enterprise policy books.

ReleaseShield AI is an autonomous release-governance system built to answer a question most teams only ask after an incident: was this change actually safe to ship? Rather than a single model producing an opaque score, the system runs a structured three-agent pipeline.

Automated, cheap checks run first; model-based judgment is reserved for the cases that require it, and is grounded in concrete evidence rather than free-form inference. What you built and what you learnt:
BreakGuard — Blast Radius & Breaking Change Detection for Pull Requests

BreakGuard is a developer tool designed to identify risks in GitHub Pull Requests that normal CI tests may miss. Instead of only checking whether existing tests pass, BreakGuard analyzes the changed code, identifies affected functions and dependent files, evaluates test coverage of the affected areas, detects potential breaking changes, and calculates an overall risk score.

The project is organized as an analysis pipeline consisting of a Diff Parser, Call Finder, Risk Scorer, and Reporter. The Diff Parser uses Tree-sitter to understand Python code and extract functions and classes. The Call Finder identifies code affected by changed functionality, while the Risk Scorer combines changed functions, affected files, untested areas, and breaking changes into a risk score and risk level. The Reporter presents the result as a clear risk report.

We also integrated the project with GitHub Actions and documented the architecture, custom agent, and custom analysis skill. The custom BreakGuard Analysis Agent provides a structured workflow for analyzing pull requests, while the PR Risk Analysis Skill defines a repeatable procedure for detecting blast-radius and breaking-change risks.

Through this project, we learned how to design a multi-stage code-analysis pipeline, work collaboratively with Git/GitHub branches and merges, use Tree-sitter for source-code analysis, integrate automated workflows with GitHub Actions, and structure agent instructions and reusable skills.

Our key takeaway is that “tests passing” does not necessarily mean a change is safe. A change can have a larger dependency blast radius than the tests reveal. BreakGuard aims to make that hidden risk visible before a pull request is merged.
Anything else for the judges:
BreakGuard focuses on a problem that is easy to overlook in conventional CI: a change can pass existing tests while still affecting a wider portion of the codebase. Sahaya AI — AI-Powered Emergency Response & Coordination
Our project, Sahaya AI, is an AI-powered emergency response system that helps connect citizens with emergency control rooms during disasters.
We noticed that during emergencies, people may send information in different forms such as text, voice, images, and location. For the emergency control room, it can be difficult to manually check every report, understand its seriousness, and decide what action should be taken.
So, we built Sahaya AI to make this process faster and more organized.
What We Built
From the citizen side, a person can use an SOS interface to:
- Enter an emergency message
- Record a voice message
- Capture or upload an image
- Share their current location
- Submit the emergency report
After submitting the report, the information is stored in our backend and given a tracking token.
The main part of our project is the AI-based triage system. Instead of directly sending every message to the emergency operator, the AI analyzes the report and provides useful information such as:
- Type of disaster
- Severity
- Priority
- Number of affected people
- Need for evacuation
- Medical requirements
- Shelter requirements
- Required resources
- Location
- Reason for the AI recommendation
The AI also classifies the report into three categories:
Emergency – when there is enough information to indicate a real emergency.
Non-Emergency – when the message is unrelated, spam, a greeting, or not an actual emergency.
Uncertain – when there is not enough information and a human needs to review it.
For example, if a citizen reports:
"Flood water has entered our village and four people are trapped on a roof. Please send help."
The system can understand this as:
Flood → Critical → People affected → Rescue required
This helps the emergency officer understand the situation quickly without reading and interpreting every report manually.
Human-in-the-Loop
One important thing we learned while building the project was that AI should not make every important decision on its own.
Therefore, we kept a Human-in-the-Loop system. The AI gives recommendations, but the Collector or emergency officer makes the final decision.
Emergency cases are shown to the Collector for approval, while uncertain cases are sent for manual review. Non-emergency reports are not allowed to directly enter the rescue workflow.
Collector / Emergency Control Room
We also created a dashboard for the Collector or emergency control room.
The dashboard allows them to view:
- Incoming SOS reports
- AI-triaged incidents
- Emergency status
- Available resources
- Dispatch information
- Weather information
The Collector can open an incident, check the AI's analysis and approve the response.
After approval, our system helps automate the next steps:
Approval → Resource Allocation → Rescue Team Assignment → Dispatch → Notification → Citizen Tracking
The citizen can then use the tracking token to check the status of their emergency response.
So, the complete workflow of our project is:
Citizen SOS → AI Triage → Incident Creation → Collector Review → Approval → Resource Allocation → Dispatch → Citizen Tracking
Technologies We Used
Frontend:
- Next.js
- React
- TypeScript
- Browser Geolocation API
- Browser Media APIs
Backend:
- Python
- FastAPI
- SQLAlchemy
- SQLite
AI:
- NVIDIA NIM
- Prompt engineering
- Structured JSON output
- Fallback logic when the AI service is unavailable
We also created automated tests for different types of reports, including emergency, non-emergency, spam, uncertain cases, fire situations, affected-person extraction, GPS location, tracking, approval and dispatch.
What We Learnt
The biggest thing we learned from this project is that building an AI application is not only about using an AI model. We also need to think about what happens before the AI processes the information and what happens after the AI gives its result.
Through this project, we learned how to:
- Convert normal human messages into structured information.
- Design AI responses that can be used for real actions.
- Handle uncertain situations instead of forcing the AI to give an answer.
- Keep humans involved when important decisions are being made.
- Use fallback methods when an external AI service is unavailable.
- Connect AI results with a database and backend workflow.
- Test the complete process instead of testing only individual screens.
Most importantly, we learned that AI can be used as a decision-support and workflow automation system, not just as a chatbot.

ARGUS is an autonomous GitHub Action that acts as an automated Senior Software Architect to review Pull Requests automatically. It executes a 3-stage evaluation pipeline:

3. Hermes (Technical Debt & Security Scanner): Inspects changed files line-by-line to flag hardcoded API keys and secrets as BLOCK warnings, unfinished TODO comments and empty function stubs as WARN alerts, and leftover debug statements like console.log as INFO notices.

ARGUS features native Google Gemini support alongside universal OpenAI-compatible cloud provider routing (NVIDIA NIM, OpenRouter, Groq Cloud, OpenAI Direct), a built-in offline fallback static analysis engine that guarantees CI pipelines never fail during API rate limits, idempotent single-comment PR thread updates, and a full web showcase with an in-browser playground simulator.

1. Agentic Workflows in CI/CD: How to divide complex code review duties into specialized persona modules (Atlas, Athena, Hermes) and execute them sequentially inside GitHub Actions.
2. Defensive AI Engineering: Production AI tools must never crash CI pipelines. Building an offline fallback static analysis engine ensured 100 percent pipeline reliability during LLM API rate limits or network outages.
3. Universal Provider Abstraction: How to abstract Google Gemini SDK and OpenAI-compatible client libraries under a single interface so developers can bring any AI provider with simple input flags.
4. Automated Code Topology: Transforming unstructured git diff data into clear, programmatically generated Mermaid.js flowcharts for instant visual comprehension.

What you built and what you learnt:
We built DevSuite — a developer productivity platform that runs a team of connected AI agents (PR Reviewer, Changelog Generator, Bug Triage, Test Scaffolding Generator) on top of a real GitHub workflow, with one core idea holding it together: a shared Decision Ledger.

Instead of agents silently acting on a repo, every proposed action (posting a PR review comment, writing a changelog entry, applying issue labels) is first logged with the agent's reasoning, confidence score, and the exact evidence it based the decision on. Nothing is applied until a human explicitly approves or rejects it from the dashboard. This gave us a genuinely auditable, human-in-the-loop system rather than a black box — every decision is traceable back to the diff, commit, or issue text that triggered it.

We built this end-to-end using an AI coding agent (Roo Code / GitHub Copilot) inside VS Code, directing it through architecture, implementation, testing, and CI setup while staying in the loop at each step — reviewing generated code, catching and fixing a broken UI state, and switching LLM providers live when our first backend ran out of free credits. That provider switch (from NVIDIA Build to Gemini) turned out to be one of the most useful things we did: it forced us to keep the LLM client cleanly abstracted in one module instead of hardcoding a provider throughout the app.

What we took away: agent-driven development is fast but not free — the agent moves quickly on well-scoped tasks, but ambiguous or multi-step requests (like "make the dashboard interactive") need to be broken into precise, verifiable steps or the agent drifts. We also learned the value of committing early and often — when our AI credits ran out mid-build, having clean, incremental commits already pushed meant we never lost real progress. Architecting for a provider switch and for a human-approval layer from the start, rather than bolting them on later, is what made both of those recoveries possible without a rewrite.
Anything else for the judges:
DevSuite was built with a swappable LLM provider layer from the start — during the event we switched the active backend from NVIDIA Build to Google Gemini without touching any agent logic, which validated that the architecture actually holds up under a real mid-build change, not just on paper.

Next steps we'd take with more time: a README Generator and a Codebase Q&A assistant, built on the same Decision Ledger pattern as the existing four agents, plus a small analytics view showing approval rates and confidence trends per agent over time.

Credits: built using VS Code with Roo Code and GitHub Copilot as coding agents, NVIDIA Build and Google AI Studio (Gemini) as LLM backends, and the GitHub REST API for all repo interactions.

What you built and what you learnt:
What We Built

We built DeCode, a command-line tool that helps developers manage their projects more efficiently — checking API health, analyzing GitHub activity, generating documentation, and (in progress) offering AI-assisted code edits, all from the terminal with human approval required before any change is applied.

We started with a much bigger idea — a CLI with an embedded AI assistant, visual flowcharts, an API checker, a doc generator, a GitHub analyzer, and a visual code editor — and quickly realized that was too much for the time we had. We cut it down to a focused core: API checking, GitHub analysis, documentation generation, and one composite `audit` command, with the AI assistant as a stretch feature layered on top once the core was solid.

We chose to build it as a CLI instead of a desktop app or web app because that's genuinely what a developer tool like this should be — something that fits into an existing terminal workflow and can run inside CI pipelines. Every command was built using Claude Code, guided by a written architecture doc, agent-rules file, and product spec we wrote before any code was generated.

What We Learnt

Cutting scope early was the best decision we made — it let us build something that actually worked and was fully tested, instead of six half-finished features. We learnt that CLI naming/package conflicts are worth checking on day one, not after the fact. We hit a real bug where our LLM calls failed with a 404 because of a missing URL segment in our Groq integration, and fixing the actual root cause (instead of guessing) saved us from repeating the mistake. We also caught a serious test bug where our test suite was accidentally reading real credentials from a developer's machine and firing live API calls — fixing that taught us a lot about test isolation.

We learnt that documenting what *isn't* built yet, honestly, is more valuable than pretending it is — it builds trust rather than costing us anything. And we learnt that having a clear, written "constitution" for how our AI agent should behave genuinely made the codebase more consistent than just prompting freely would have.

Overall, this project taught us that good engineering discipline — specify first, test continuously, diagnose root causes, and be honest about what's done — matters more than any single technology choice.
Anything else for the judges:
A Note to the Judges

We want to draw your attention to a few things in our repository that we think are easy to miss if you only look at the final feature list, but which we believe are the actual substance of what you're evaluating.

First, our commit history isn't just a build log — it's a record of real engineering decisions made under real constraints. If you check our CI history, you'll see we caught and fixed a live bug where our LLM integration was silently failing with a 404 due to a missing URL segment, and separately caught a test-isolation issue where our test suite was accidentally reading real credentials from a developer's machine. We didn't just patch these — we added regression tests specifically so they can't silently reappear. We'd genuinely encourage you to look at those specific commits over the polish of any single command's output, because we think they say more about how we work than a clean demo does.

Second, we made a deliberate choice to under-promise in our documentation rather than over-promise. Anywhere a feature was designed but not yet fully built, our README and PRD say so explicitly, in plain language, rather than describing it as complete. We'd rather you catch us being conservative than catch us overstating something — we'd like our documentation to be something you can trust at face value when you're reviewing it under time pressure.

Third, we cut real scope early. Our original idea had twice as many features as what we shipped. We chose to build a smaller set of things well, fully tested, with CI genuinely green, rather than a longer feature list that was shakier under the surface. We think that's the harder and more defensible choice, and we made it consciously rather than by running out of time.

If you have questions about any specific design decision — why we chose a CLI over a desktop app, why we deferred certain features, or how our AI assistant's safety approval flow works — we'd welcome the chance to walk through the reasoning directly. Thank you for your time reviewing our work.

AccrediLens is a local-first AI accreditation audit agent designed to reduce the time and manual effort required for NBA and NAAC compliance reviews.

Institutions normally work with lengthy Self-Assessment Reports, accreditation manuals, and supporting documents. Reviewers must manually examine hundreds of pages, locate evidence for each criterion, verify whether that evidence is sufficient, and identify missing documentation. AccrediLens turns this into a structured, evidence-grounded agent workflow.

The system allows a user to upload institutional PDFs, including scanned documents. It extracts and structures their content, divides it into searchable passages, and indexes the evidence for semantic retrieval. For each selected accreditation criterion, the agent interprets the requirement, searches the institutional documents, retrieves the most relevant supporting passages, preserves page-level citations, evaluates the sufficiency of the available evidence, and highlights compliance gaps requiring corrective action. The output is intended to be auditable: conclusions are linked back to source passages rather than being presented as unsupported AI-generated answers.

AccrediLens uses a Next.js frontend and a FastAPI backend, with PostgreSQL for application data, Redis for supporting services, Qdrant for vector retrieval, and Ollama for local language-model inference. Its local-first architecture helps institutions analyse potentially sensitive academic documents without unnecessarily sending them to external AI services. The repository includes reproducible setup instructions, architecture documentation, dependency files, demonstration evidence, startup and shutdown scripts, agent capability documentation, and automated browser testing.

A GitHub Actions CI pipeline validates Docker Compose configuration, backend dependencies and Python compilation, PowerShell lifecycle scripts, TypeScript, ESLint, the production frontend build, and Playwright smoke tests in Chromium. The latest workflow is passing.

While building AccrediLens, we learnt that accreditation analysis is not simply a document-chat problem. Reliable auditing requires criterion decomposition, multi-stage retrieval, source traceability, evidence-sufficiency assessment, and a clear distinction between missing evidence and actual non-compliance. We also learnt the importance of local AI, reproducible infrastructure, automated testing, and transparent citations when designing agents for high-stakes institutional decision support.
Anything else for the judges:
AccrediLens is designed as an evidence-grounded audit assistant, not a generic PDF chatbot. Its principal contribution is the agentic workflow that maps institutional evidence to individual NBA/NAAC requirements, returns page-level supporting citations, evaluates evidence sufficiency, and exposes documentation gaps for human review.

The system is intentionally human-in-the-loop: its findings support accreditation teams and auditors but do not claim to replace the final judgement of an authorised NBA or NAAC evaluator.

DevCloud is a self-hosted, open-source alternative to Vercel/Railway for
developers who want GitOps deployments without handing their code to a

I built it end-to-end using the Agent-Driven Lifecycle: started with a
constitution.md defining non-negotiable rules for the agent (human review
before infra changes, empirical verification via build/lint/test before
declaring anything done, conventional commits, zero hardcoded secrets),
then wrote the PRD and architecture spec before any implementation began.
From there the agent built the backend module by module — auth, team
management, the deployment engine, GitHub webhook integration — then the
frontend, then CI/CD and Docker Compose for production. I committed
progressively through each phase rather than in one dump, so the git
history reads as the actual build order.

I also defined a custom agent (a Cloud Architect persona focused on
container topology, Traefik routing, and Prisma migration safety) and a
custom skill (a Deployment Verifier that checks container health, SSL
issuance, and webhook delivery) — both documented in AGENTS_AND_SKILLS.md.

What I took away: the hardest part of agent-driven building isn't getting
code written, it's catching what the agent gets subtly wrong without you
noticing — a stale product name left in one file after a rename, a test
that passes without actually testing anything, a CI step that's quietly
configured to never fail. Writing the constitution up front helped, but it
didn't replace actually reading every file before committing it. That's
the main thing I'd do more of with more time.

PART 1: WHAT I BUILT
----------------------------------------------------------------

I built InvoicePilot AI — a tool that automates a job almost
every company deals with: reading incoming invoices, checking
them for problems, and deciding whether they're safe to pay or
need a person to look at them first.

The problem I wanted to solve

Before something like this exists, that job is done by hand.
Someone in an accounts department opens an invoice — an email
attachment, a scanned PDF, sometimes even a photo of a paper
invoice — and manually types the details into a spreadsheet or
accounting system: vendor name, invoice number, date, amount,
tax number, and so on. Then they have to eyeball whether it looks
right, check if it matches an approved purchase order, and decide
what to do with it.

This is slow. It's boring, repetitive work, which means people
get tired and careless. And it's genuinely risky — companies lose
real money because someone misses a duplicate invoice (the same
bill submitted twice, sometimes on purpose, to try and get paid
twice), or misses that a tax number is missing, or approves
something too quickly because they're rushing to clear a pile of
invoices before lunch.

I wanted to build something that could do this reading-and-
checking work automatically, quickly, and consistently — but
without removing the human from the important decisions. I didn't
want to build a system where an AI just decides things and nobody
can explain why.

How it actually works, step by step

Here's the simple version of what happens when someone uses the
app:

1. You give it an invoice — a PDF, a photo, or even just pasted
   text copied from an email.

2. An AI model reads the document and pulls out the important
   details: vendor name, invoice number, invoice date, total
   amount, tax number, purchase order number, and the individual
   line items on the bill.

3. Then a set of clear, plain-logic rules — not the AI, rules I
   wrote myself — check the extracted invoice:
   - Is anything missing that should be there, like a vendor
     name or an invoice number?
   - Have we seen this exact invoice before? That's a duplicate.
   - Does it break any company policy — for example, does a
     large invoice need a purchase order attached, and does it
     have one?
   - Is this a brand-new vendor we've never dealt with before,
     which naturally carries a bit more risk than an established
     one?
   - Taking all of that together, how risky does this invoice
     look overall, on a scale from low to critical?

4. Based on all of that, the system reaches one of three
   outcomes: auto-approve it because it's clearly fine, send it
   to a human to review because something needs a second look, or
   reject it outright because it clearly breaks a rule.

5. Anything that needs a human shows up in an "Approvals" screen
   inside the app. A real person can open it, see exactly why it
   was flagged — not just "risky," but the specific reason — and
   click Approve or Reject. That decision, along with who made it
   and when, is permanently recorded.

6. Every invoice ever processed, and every step the system took
   to reach its decision, gets saved. You can go back to any
   invoice later and see the full story — what was read out of
   the document, what checks were run, what was flagged, and what
   the final decision was and by whom.

7. There's also a small AI chat assistant built into the app. You
   can ask it plain questions about a processed invoice, like
   "why was this one flagged?" or "what's the total tax on this
   bill?", and it answers using the real data from that specific
   invoice, not a generic guess.

The technology behind it

On the backend — the part that does the actual thinking and
processing — I used Python with a framework called FastAPI, which
handles incoming requests (like "process this invoice") and sends
back structured responses. It reads PDFs and images using a
library called PyMuPDF. For the actual AI reading step, it
connects to multiple AI providers — Google Gemini, Groq, and
NVIDIA — and if one of them is slow or having problems, it
automatically tries the next one instead of just failing. That
felt important: a real business tool can't just stop working
because one AI provider is temporarily down.

On the frontend — what the user actually sees and clicks on — I
used React with TypeScript, which is a safer version of
JavaScript that catches a lot of mistakes before the code even
runs. It's styled with Tailwind CSS and built using a tool called
Vite. I also built an offline "demo mode" into the frontend, so
the interface can be explored and shown off even without a live
connection to the backend — useful for demos where internet or
server uptime can't always be guaranteed.

For testing, I wrote automated tests for the backend logic using
a tool called pytest — these test the actual business rules
(validation, duplicate detection, policy checks, risk scoring)
directly, with fake sample invoices, without needing any AI
connection at all. I also have end-to-end tests using a tool
called Playwright, which actually opens a real browser and clicks
through the app the way a real user would, to make sure the whole
thing genuinely works together, not just in pieces.

All of this — the tests, the build process — runs automatically
every time I push new code, using GitHub Actions. That means I
find out immediately if something's broken, instead of only
discovering it later when it's harder to fix.

The most important decision I made

If I had to pick the single most important choice in the whole
project, it's this: I decided the AI is only allowed to do one
job — reading and understanding the raw invoice document. Every
decision that happens after that — is anything missing, is this a
duplicate, does it break a rule, how risky is it, should a human
look at it — is handled by plain, ordinary logic that I wrote and
can explain line by line. Nothing important happens just because
"the AI said so." I think that distinction is what separates a
fun demo from something a real company could actually trust with
real money.


PART 2: WHAT I LEARNED
----------------------------------------------------------------

1. Building something that works is not the same as building
   something that's ready to show someone.

My code worked fairly early on — the pipeline ran end to end,
invoices got processed, results appeared on screen, it looked
impressive in a quick demo. But when I actually sat down and
checked my project against what judges would specifically be
looking for, I found real gaps underneath that surface: there was
no architecture document explaining how the pieces fit together,
no written rules describing how AI coding tools should behave
inside my own repository, no automated tests at all for the
backend, and only a small piece of a CI/CD pipeline instead of a
complete one. The app "worked" on my own laptop, but that's a
very different and much lower bar than "a stranger can open this
repository, understand what's going on, trust that it works, and
actually verify that for themselves." That was a genuinely
useful realization: documentation and tests aren't polish you add
at the end if you have time left over. They're what actually
turns working code into something someone else can rely on and
evaluate fairly.

2. Small naming mistakes can quietly break things that "obviously"
work.
Anything else for the judges:
WHY THIS PROBLEM
----------------------------------------------------------------

I picked invoice processing on purpose, not because it's flashy,
but because it's real. Almost every company, no matter how small
or large, has someone doing this job by hand right now: opening
invoices, typing details into a system, checking for mistakes,
deciding what to pay. It's not a made-up problem for a demo — it's
one of the most common examples of "repetitive, multi-step,
manual work" that Track A specifically asks us to rebuild. I
wanted to build something that could genuinely be handed to a
real accounts team, not just something that looks good on a
projector for three minutes.


HOW THIS MAPS TO WHAT'S BEING JUDGED
----------------------------------------------------------------

Rather than describe the project in the abstract, here's how I
think about it against each judged area:

Specification and Architecture
  ARCHITECTURE.md lays out the stack, the data model, and the
  9-step pipeline. AGENTS_AND_SKILLS.md documents the custom
  agent and every custom skill, and explains why they're genuinely
  custom logic rather than generic boilerplate. PRD.md covers user
  stories and acceptance criteria — what a user should be able to
  do, and how we'd know it's working correctly.

Working Software and Delivery
  The app runs end to end, locally and via Docker, and is
  deployed live: frontend on GitHub Pages, backend deployable to
  Render with a committed render.yaml blueprint so the deployment
  itself is reproducible from the repo, not something only I can
  do from memory.

Agent Engineering and Code Quality
  This is where I put the most thought. The agent (InvoiceAgent)
  and its planner handle ordering, retries, and required-vs-
  optional steps. Every one of the 9 skills is a thin adapter
  around real, testable business logic — validators, a policy
  engine, a risk engine, a duplicate detector — not a single big
  prompt asking an AI model to "just handle it."

Testing and Verification
  Backend logic has real pytest coverage: validators, policy
  rules, risk scoring, duplicate detection, the planner's step
  ordering, and an API smoke test. The frontend has a Playwright
  end-to-end suite that drives the actual UI in a real browser.
  Both run automatically in CI on every push, and the Playwright
  report is uploaded as a CI artifact so it can be inspected
  after the fact, not just trusted on faith.


WHAT MAKES THIS DIFFERENT FROM "JUST CALLING AN AI MODEL"
----------------------------------------------------------------

I want to be direct about this because I think it's the most
important thing to understand about the project: the AI model is
used in exactly one place — reading a messy document and turning
it into structured data. Every decision after that point is
ordinary, readable code that I wrote and can point to directly.
If a judge asks "why was this invoice flagged," the honest answer
is never "the AI decided" — it's a specific rule, in a specific
file, with a specific reason attached to it in the audit log.

I think this matters beyond just being good engineering practice.
A system that automates financial decisions and can't explain
itself is a liability, not a feature. A system that can show its
work, and that refuses to finalize anything risky without a human
saying yes, is something a real business could actually adopt.
That was the standard I was building toward, not just "does it
work in the demo."

What you built and what you learnt:
What We Built
ReadMyCode is an AI-powered code analysis and documentation platform. You paste a public GitHub repository URL (or upload a ZIP archive), and it instantly generates:

A comprehensive README document
Structured API documentation with endpoint schemas
Interactive flowchart diagrams showing control flow
Architecture diagrams mapping system components
Function-by-function explanations with complexity analysis
A code debugger that performs static analysis for bugs
The entire platform is deployed live on Vercel at https://read-my-code.vercel.app and the source code is at https://github.com/akshatanand-cell/ReadMyCode.

The Problem
Every developer knows the pain: you build something great, but documenting it is tedious. README files are outdated, API docs don't exist, and onboarding new contributors means walking them through the code manually. We wanted to make documentation as effortless as pasting a link.

How We Built It
Tech Stack
Frontend: React 18 + Vite 5, Tailwind CSS, Mermaid.js for diagram rendering
Backend: Express.js (Node 18+), REST API with JWT authentication
AI Engine: xAI Grok API (grok-2-latest) for code understanding and generation
Database: MongoDB with Mongoose, plus a custom zero-dependency MemoryStore fallback
Deployment: Vercel (static frontend + serverless API functions)
Testing: Playwright end-to-end tests with HTML report artifacts
CI/CD: GitHub Actions pipeline with Node 18/20 matrix, ESLint, build verification, and Playwright
Architecture Decisions
1. The AI Agent System We built a custom CodeAnalyzer Agent (documented in AGENTS_AND_SKILLS.md) that takes parsed source code and routes it through type-specific prompts to the Grok API. Each analysis type — readme, apiDocs, flowchart, architecture, functionExplain, debug — has a strict output contract. If the AI returns a README when we asked for a Mermaid diagram, our parser detects the mismatch and triggers the fallback engine.

The fallback engine is critical: it guarantees that the UI always renders something useful. If the AI API is down, rate-limited, or returns garbage, we generate valid placeholder content matching the expected format. The user never sees a blank screen or a raw error.

2. The MermaidDiagramSkill Our custom MermaidDiagramSkill is a dual-mode diagram renderer. It first attempts Mermaid.js v10.9 rendering with suppressErrorRendering: true. If the syntax is invalid (which happens often with LLM-generated diagrams), it automatically falls back to an interactive SVG renderer that parses node names from the raw text, lays them out in an animated grid, and draws gradient connections between them — complete with pan, zoom, and hover effects. We also added a CSS-level DOM shield that purges Mermaid's error elements from document.body.

3. Three-Tier Repository Cloning The RepoCloner Agent uses a 3-tier fallback strategy that guarantees success:

Tier 1: git clone --depth 1 via simple-git (fastest, requires git binary)
Tier 2: ZIP download from codeload.github.com (works without git, tries main then master branches)
Tier 3: Mock repository structure (absolute last resort, always succeeds)
This was essential for Vercel deployment where git binaries may not be available.

4. Zero-Dependency Database Fallback We built a custom in-memory MemoryStore (server/utils/memoryStore.js) that mirrors the Mongoose API (create, findById, save, deleteOne). When MongoDB is unavailable — which is always the case on Vercel's serverless functions — the app transparently switches to MemoryStore. Every controller checks mongoose.connection.readyState === 1 and branches accordingly. Users never know the difference.

The Agent-Driven Development Process
The entire application was built using an AI coding agent following strict rules defined in our AGENTS.md constitution. Key rules include:

Server code in CommonJS, client code in ES Modules
Every async controller wrapped in try/catch with structured JSON errors
AI failures must fall back to generateFallbackContent() — never return empty results
File operations use os.tmpdir() in serverless environments
Progressive commits with conventional format (feat:, fix:, docs:, test:, ci:)
The agent worked through a phased task breakdown (documented in TASK_BREAKDOWN.md): core backend → GitHub integration → AI engine → frontend → UI redesign → diagram fixes → Vercel deployment → hackathon requirements.

Challenges & Solutions
Vercel Serverless Filesystem: Vercel functions have a read-only filesystem except /tmp. Our initial code wrote cloned repos to ./temp_repos inside the app directory, which crashed with EROFS: read-only file system. Fix: replaced all file paths with path.join(os.tmpdir(), "readmycode_repos").

MongoMemoryServer Binary Timeout: We originally used mongodb-memory-server as a DB fallback, but it downloads a 600MB mongod binary at runtime — impossible in a serverless function with 10-second cold starts. Fix: removed it entirely and built the lightweight MemoryStore.

Build-Time vs Runtime API URL: Vite statically compiles import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL at build time. Since VITE_API_URL wasn't set during Vercel's build, it hardcoded http://localhost:5000/api into the production bundle. Fix: wrapped the URL resolution in a runtime function that checks window.location.hostname first.

LLM Output Unpredictability: The Grok API sometimes returns Markdown when asked for Mermaid syntax, or wraps JSON in code fences. Fix: built robust parsers that strip code fences, validate output format against the expected type contract, and trigger fallback generation on any mismatch.

What We Learned
Serverless is a different paradigm. You can't assume a writable filesystem, persistent processes, or pre-installed binaries. Every assumption from traditional Node.js development breaks. Designing for ephemeral, stateless execution from the start would have saved us hours of debugging.

LLM outputs need defensive parsing. AI models don't follow instructions perfectly. Building a robust fallback system that guarantees valid output regardless of what the API returns is not optional — it's the core engineering challenge of any AI-powered product.

Agent-driven development works, but needs guardrails. Having an AI agent build the app was incredibly productive, but the AGENTS.md constitution was essential. Without explicit rules about error handling, file paths, and commit hygiene, the agent would take shortcuts that break in production.

Progressive deployment beats big-bang releases. Pushing small, focused commits and testing on Vercel after each one let us isolate failures instantly. A single massive commit would have been impossible to debug.

The gap between "works locally" and "works in production" is where real engineering lives. Our app ran perfectly on localhost from day one. Making it work on Vercel required solving filesystem constraints, binary availability, build-time vs runtime evaluation, CORS origins, and cold start timeouts — none of which exist locally.
Anything else for the judges:
Known Issues
Vercel Serverless Statelessness: Since Vercel serverless functions are ephemeral, the MemoryStore resets on every cold start. Previously analyzed repos don't persist across deployments. This is by design for the hackathon — production would use MongoDB Atlas.

Large Repositories: Repos with 1000+ files may hit the 30-second serverless timeout. The AI context window also has token limits, so very large codebases get truncated to the most important files (entry points, configs, route handlers).

Mermaid Syntax from LLMs: AI-generated Mermaid diagrams are syntactically invalid ~30% of the time. Our interactive SVG fallback handles this gracefully, but the fallback diagrams are less detailed than properly parsed Mermaid output. We're working on a post-processing layer that auto-corrects common Mermaid syntax errors before rendering.

Private Repositories: Currently only public GitHub repos are supported without a personal access token. The architecture supports token-based auth (GITHUB_TOKEN env var), but we haven't built a UI flow for users to provide their own tokens.

What We Would Do Next
Short-term (Week 1-2):

Connect MongoDB Atlas for persistent storage across deployments
Add a "Copy to Clipboard" and "Download as PDF" button for all generated content
Implement real-time streaming of AI responses (SSE) so users see content generating live instead of waiting for the full response
Add support for GitLab and Bitbucket URLs alongside GitHub
Medium-term (Month 1):

Build a VS Code extension that generates docs directly from the editor
Add collaborative features — share analysis results via public links
Implement diff-aware re-analysis: when a repo is updated, only re-analyze changed files
Add support for private repos via OAuth GitHub login
Long-term Vision:

Multi-model support (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini) with automatic quality comparison
A "Documentation CI" GitHub Action that auto-generates and commits docs on every PR
Team workspaces with role-based access and org-level analytics
An SDK/API so other tools can plug into ReadMyCode's analysis engine
Technical Decisions Worth Highlighting
Why Grok (xAI) over GPT-4 or Claude? Grok-2 offered the best balance of speed, cost, and code understanding for this use case. Its response latency is consistently under 3 seconds for our prompts, and it handles multi-language codebases (JS, Python, Go, Rust) without quality degradation. The API is also simpler to integrate — no complex tokenizer setup or streaming boilerplate.

Why a custom MemoryStore instead of SQLite/Redis? We needed a zero-dependency, zero-binary fallback that works identically on localhost and Vercel serverless. SQLite requires native binaries (won't compile on Vercel). Redis requires an external service. Our MemoryStore is 113 lines of pure JavaScript that mirrors the Mongoose API — no dependencies, no binaries, instant startup.

Why Mermaid.js + SVG fallback instead of D3 or Cytoscape? Mermaid.js is the industry standard for text-to-diagram rendering and integrates naturally with AI-generated output. But LLMs produce invalid Mermaid syntax frequently, so we built the SVG fallback as an insurance policy. The dual-mode approach means diagrams always render — users never see a broken page.

What you built and what you learnt:
MIGRATE: Legacy Python Equivalence Converter

What it does:
MIGRATE is a production-grade GitHub Action that automatically migrates legacy Python 2 codebases to Python 3 — and mathematically proves the migrated code behaves identically to the original. It solves the "silent hallucination" problem that plagues every existing AI migration tool: the converter can lie, but the sandbox cannot.

How it works (the pipeline):
1. CLASSIFY — An AST-based classifier triages every top-level function into one of three buckets: template_match (simple syntax renames), llm_needed (complex semantic refactoring), or unsupported (flagged and skipped). This prevents expensive LLM calls on trivial changes.

2. CONVERT — Template-matched functions go through a zero-hallucination regex engine that handles all standard Python 2→3 idioms: cPickle→pickle, xrange→range, print statements, integer division, dict.iterkeys(), old-style exception syntax, octal literals, and more. Complex functions are sent to our dual-LLM architecture: Gemini 1.5 Flash performs deep semantic refactoring, and NVIDIA MiniMax acts as an adversarial critic to catch any hallucinations before they proceed.

3. VERIFY — The crown jewel. The original Python 2 function and the converted Python 3 function are both executed inside isolated Docker containers (python:2.7-slim and python:3.12-slim) against Hypothesis-generated fuzz fixtures. Outputs are compared using DeepDiff. Only an exact_match on all cases produces a PASS verdict. A behavioral drift is a hard FAIL — no exceptions.

4. REPORT — Every function (pass, fail, or needs-review) is surfaced in build/summary.json and as a GitHub Actions workflow summary. Ambiguous functions are posted as PR comments without blocking the pipeline, preserving visibility and human control.

5. AUTO-COMMIT — Verified, passing Python 3 code is automatically committed back to the repository's migrated/ directory, creating a clean, reviewable migration history.

How we built it:
Built in Python with a strict multi-agent contract defined via shared/schemas.py (Pydantic). The CLI orchestrator (cli/convert.py) implements all pipeline rules from AGENTS.md. Each "agent" (Classifier, Converter+Critic, Verifier) has a defined input/output schema and can be developed and tested independently. The full system is packaged as a composite GitHub Action (action.yml) and published to the GitHub Marketplace.

What we learnt:
The most important lesson: behavioral equivalence is harder than syntactic correctness. An LLM can produce Python 3 code that runs perfectly but returns a list where the original returned a generator — and a code review will never catch it. Only execution in isolated containers against the same inputs catches this. We also learnt that strict agent contracts (never let a conversion_failed function reach the verifier, never call the LLM for a template_match function) make a multi-agent system dramatically more debuggable than one where agents have overlapping responsibilities. Finally: PowerShell's echo command writes UTF-16. Always use Set-Content -Encoding UTF8.
Anything else for the judges:
Known limitations:
- The Docker-based verifier requires functions to be independently executable with generated fixtures. Functions with heavy side effects (database writes, network calls) are currently classified as needs_review rather than auto-verified, since fixture generation cannot safely stub external dependencies.
- The Hypothesis fixture generator uses type annotations where available and falls back to heuristic type inference. Functions with complex custom types may produce lower-quality fixtures.

What we would do next:
- Add a feedback loop: when the NVIDIA critic flags a conversion, feed its reasoning back to Gemini for a second-pass correction before escalating to needs_review.
- Extend the template engine to handle async/await patterns (Python 2 codebases migrating to modern async Python 3).
- Add a web dashboard to visualize migration progress across an entire organization's repositories.
- Support JavaScript/TypeScript → modern ES2024 migrations using the same sandbox-diff architecture.

What you built and what you learnt:
We built a CI gate that catches AI-generated tests that look fine but don't actually test anything. The idea started from a problem all four of us have hit: an AI agent writes code, then writes tests for that code, and the tests pass but half the time they're just calling the function and not checking what it returns. Nothing in a normal CI pipeline catches that.
So our gate does something a bit sneaky: it takes the demo code, quietly injects five specific bugs into it (flips an == to !=, shifts a boundary, drops a null check, that kind of thing), and reruns the existing test suite against the broken code. If the tests still pass, that mutant "survived"  which means the tests were never actually checking that behavior in the first place. If even one mutant survives, the gate blocks the merge, no matter how green the original test run looked.
We split ownership across the stack: the mutation engine and gate logic, the LLM explainer and API, the frontend, and the docs/architecture/deployment side each had an owner, with an AGENTS.md file in the repo laying out folder ownership and hard rules (fail closed, never let the LLM hang the gate, five operators exactly and no scope creep) so our AI coding agents stayed inside their lane instead of quietly rewriting each other's work. When a mutant does survive, we pass it to an LLM (Gemini, with a templated fallback if the API call fails or times out) to generate a plain-English explanation of the specific missing assertion  not just "tests are weak," but "you're missing an assertion for the None case at line 58."
What we actually learnt was less about mutation testing and more about the gap between "the AI wrote code that runs" and "the AI wrote code that's actually correct." Getting the fail-closed behavior right making sure a timeout, a crashed subprocess, or a missing API key always defaults to blocking the merge rather than silently passing took more care than the mutation logic itself. We also learnt the hard way that documentation drifts fast under time pressure: more than once our own AGENTS_AND_SKILLS.md ended up describing a mechanism (AST-based operators) that didn't match what we'd actually shipped (plain string matching) a small irony for a project whose entire premise is "don't trust what looks right without checking it.
Anything else for the judges:
A few things we want to be upfront about rather than let you discover mid-review:

The LLM explainer has a fail-safe path by design: if the Gemini call errors or times out, it falls back to a templated explanation so the gate never hangs. Right now that fallback is firing more often than we'd like in the deployed version, so a couple of the mutant explanations you'll see are template text rather than freshly generated ones. The mechanism works as designed; we'd tune the reliability of the live LLM call next.

The backend runs on Render's free tier, so if it's been idle, the first request can take 30-50 seconds to wake up. If the demo looks stuck on first load, that's why; give it a moment.

Next on our list: making the LLM call more robust (it currently only reads the first response segment from the API, which can truncate longer explanations), tightening up the CSS/theming (we've got two half-reconciled systems in there), and pinning dependency versions more carefully.

What you built and what you learnt:
Artemis: Project Retrospective
1. Executive Summary
Artemis is an AI Interview Copilot that records Google Meet audio via a Chrome extension, transcribes it in real-time, and uses Mistral LLM to objectively score candidate performance. It consists of a React/Vite dashboard (Vercel), a Node.js/WS backend (Railway), and a Manifest V3 Chrome Extension.

2. Infrastructure & Architecture Pivot
We initially planned a serverless deployment for the entire monorepo on Vercel. However, serverless environments inherently terminate long-lived connections. We extracted the Express backend into a standalone repository and deployed it to Railway. This pivot was critical, allowing persistent WebSockets to continuously stream interview audio without timeouts.

3. Chrome Extension (Manifest V3)
Chrome’s MV3 security model replaced persistent background pages with ephemeral Service Workers that lack access to DOM APIs like MediaRecorder. Solution: We leveraged the Offscreen Document API. The Service Worker routes logic, while a hidden offscreen document captures the active tab's audio, processes it into 16kHz PCM chunks, and streams it to our backend via WebSockets.

4. WebSockets, Deepgram & Mistral
Real-time STT: As the backend receives audio, it acts as a low-latency proxy, streaming the data to Deepgram for Speech-to-Text. We capture diarized text (separating interviewer vs. candidate) and push it back to the UI live. LLM Evaluation: Upon completion, the full transcript is sent to Mistral via REST. By strictly enforcing JSON-mode (response_format: json_object), we prevent LLM hallucinations and receive a deterministic object containing scores and structured feedback.

5. UI, UX, & Typography
The React dashboard was optimized for speed (Vite) and aesthetics (Tailwind CSS, Recharts for dynamic radar charts). We implemented a self-hosted dual-font system (Lost Saloon for bold headers, Elegant Typewriter for body text), eliminating Google Fonts dependencies, improving privacy, and preventing Cumulative Layout Shifts (CLS).

6. Database & Authentication
We paired Supabase (Postgres/Auth) with Drizzle ORM. Auth: The Chrome extension securely syncs Supabase JWTs via PKCE flow, validating every WS/REST request. ORM: Drizzle provided strict compile-time TypeScript safety for all database mutations, replacing error-prone raw SQL queries.

7. CI/CD & Code Quality
We elevated Artemis to a production-grade standard:

Husky & lint-staged: Enforces Prettier formatting on every commit, ensuring uniform code style across the repo.
Playwright: Configured end-to-end tests that run on GitHub Actions, spinning up headless Chromium to verify deployment health automatically on every push.
8. Key Engineering Learnings
Match Infrastructure to Protocol: Serverless fails for WebSockets; persistent containers (Railway) are mandatory for real-time streaming.
MV3 Requires Separation of Concerns: Service Workers handle state and routing; Offscreen documents handle DOM APIs.
LLMs as Deterministic Functions: Enforcing strict JSON outputs allows LLMs to act as reliable pipeline components rather than unpredictable chatbots.
Automate Quality: CI/CD and pre-commit hooks pay immediate dividends by catching regressions and eliminating formatting debates.

What you built and what you learnt:
What it does:
The Incident RCA Agent bridges the critical gap between incident detection and resolution. When a system goes down, observability tools tell you what is broken, but the 10-hour manual log-parsing process to figure out why is where engineering time is lost. This tool ingests raw, chaotic, multi-source server logs (Application, Database, and Kubernetes infrastructure), deterministically extracts the root cause with zero-hallucination citations, and instantly converts that analysis into structured, actionable Jira tickets. It doesn't just help SREs survive the outage; it operationalizes the learnings so the exact same outage never happens again.

How it was built:
The application is built on a modular, three-tier Python architecture designed for resilience and enterprise scalability:

Presentation Layer (ui.py): A Streamlit-based frontend utilizing a strict state machine (idle -> uploaded -> generated -> revision -> approved -> jira) to enforce a Human-in-the-Loop workflow. It features real-time token streaming and a "Phantom" Jira push to demonstrate the end-to-end UX without risking live API failures during the demo.
Reasoning Engine (rca_agent.py): The core brain interacting with the Google Gemini API. To prevent the common LLM failure mode where generating long text corrupts strict JSON formatting, I engineered a Two-Call Pipeline. Call 1 streams the narrative RCA (Executive Summary, Timeline, Root Cause) using highly token-optimized, telegraphic prompts. Call 2 is a blocking call that extracts minified JSON Action Items from the completed narrative.
Data & Export Layer (jira_skill.py): Because LLM outputs are non-deterministic, I built a defensive, deterministic parser. It uses a custom bracket-matching algorithm (ignoring citation brackets like [Log Line 3]) and a sanitization step to fix trailing commas and literal newlines, ensuring 100% valid JSON extraction into a Pandas DataFrame.
Free-Tier Resilience: To ensure the app runs flawlessly on the free tier without hitting 429 Rate Limit errors, I implemented a thread-safe Leaky Bucket rate limiter, SHA-256 deterministic caching (so identical log analyses cost zero tokens), and jittered exponential backoff via the tenacity library.
What I learnt:

AI Output is Untrusted Data: The biggest takeaway is that you cannot trust an LLM to format data perfectly. Building the robust, fallback-heavy JSON parser in jira_skill.py taught me that defensive programming is just as important in AI engineering as it is in traditional backend development.
Prompt Engineering is Structural, Not Just Linguistic: I learned that managing token budgets requires forcing the LLM into strict structural constraints (e.g., forcing minified JSON, enforcing [Log Line X] citations, and programmatically prepending line numbers to logs) rather than just asking it nicely to be concise.
Separation of Concerns Enables Scale: By strictly decoupling the ingestion layer (UI) from the reasoning engine (rca_agent.py), I learned how to design AI applications that can be scaled from a single-file MVP to a distributed Map-Reduce architecture in V2 without rewriting the core product logic.
Anything else for the judges:
Known Issues & Architectural Trade-offs (MVP):

Context Window Limits: The current MVP processes logs as a single string. While optimized to handle ~2,500 lines (approx 250KB) efficiently, uploading a massive 500MB core dump will hit the LLM's context window and trigger a truncation warning. This was a deliberate MVP trade-off to perfect the reasoning logic before implementing distributed chunking.
State Management: The Streamlit frontend uses in-memory session state, making it single-user. This was chosen for rapid UX validation over building a full backend for the hackathon timeline.
Jira Integration: The "Push to Jira" button in the UI is currently a mocked integration to demonstrate the end-to-end UX flow safely. Direct integration with Jira's REST API v3 requires mapping to their complex Atlassian Document Format (ADF), which is planned for V2.
V2 Roadmap (Next Steps):

Map-Reduce Log Chunking: Implement LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter to chunk massive log files, process them in parallel, and synthesize the root cause, pushing past the context window limits.
Adapter Pattern for Ticketing: Build a JiraAdapter and LinearAdapter to map our clean Pandas DataFrame output directly into their respective proprietary API schemas (like Jira's ADF).
Enterprise Security (PII Redaction): Add a deterministic pre-processing step using local Regex/NER to scrub IP addresses, DB credentials, and customer IDs before the prompt is ever sent to the LLM.
Private VPC Deployment: Migrate from the public Google AI Studio API to Google Cloud Vertex AI to allow deployment inside a private VPC with zero public internet egress, satisfying enterprise compliance requirements.

What we built:

We built Chiron, an AI-powered multi-agent system designed to automate and streamline airline baggage claim evaluations. The manual claim resolution process is notoriously slow, prone to human error, and lacks consistent policy application. Chiron solves this by introducing a deterministic, four-step AI agent pipeline that evaluates claims instantly while maintaining a "Human-in-the-Loop" safety net.


Our pipeline consists of 4 specialized agents:

Ingestion Agent: Parses raw claim data (flight details, PNR, damage descriptions).

Fraud Audit Agent: Analyzes the claim for suspicious patterns or anomalies, generating a Fraud Risk Score.

Policy Engine Agent: Cross-references the claim against airline compensation policies to determine a mathematically backed, recommended payout.

Response Drafter Agent: Synthesizes the previous outputs into a professional, empathetic, and personalized email draft for the passenger.


How we built it:

Backend: Python and FastAPI. We orchestrated a multi-agent architecture where each agent has a single, verifiable responsibility, preventing LLM hallucinations.

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. We designed a sleek dashboard that allows claims adjusters to review the AI's logic, see the fraud score, and approve the final payout and email draft.

Integration: The frontend seamlessly communicates with the Python agents via a REST API.


What we learnt:

The Power of Agentic Workflows: We learned that breaking down a massive LLM prompt into smaller, sequential, and deterministic agents drastically improves accuracy and makes debugging much easier.

Cross-Stack Integration: We successfully bridged a modern Node.js/React frontend with a robust Python backend, handling cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) and API payload mapping under strict time constraints.

AI with Accountability: We realized that in enterprise solutions (like insurance or claims), AI shouldn't just give an answer—it must show its work. Building an audit trail into our agents was a major learning curve.
Anything else for the judges:
Known Issues:

Because we are using free-tier hosting platforms for deployment, there might be a slight "cold start" delay of 30-50 seconds when evaluating the very first claim. Subsequent claims process instantly.

What we would do next (Future Scope):

Real-time Flight Integrations: Integrate with live flight APIs (like FlightAware) to automatically verify if a flight was delayed or canceled before processing the claim.

RAG Vector Database: Implement a dedicated vector database for airline policies so that non-technical staff can upload PDF updates and the AI instantly adapts its logic.

Analytics Dashboard: Add a view to track fleet-wide baggage damage trends and fraud detection rates over time.

What you built and what you learnt:
Introduction
Working on the Operon – Invoice-to-Pay project was a valuable learning experience
because it allowed me to understand how software development, artificial
intelligence, automation, and real-world business processes can be combined into
one practical application. Before working on this project, I mainly understood
programming and web development as separate technical concepts. Through this
project, I learned that developing a useful software system requires much more than
writing code. It requires understanding the actual problem, breaking it into smaller
components, designing an appropriate architecture, deciding where automation
should be applied, considering where human intervention is necessary, and making
sure that the final system is understandable and reliable for its users.
The main purpose of Operon is to automate repetitive tasks involved in the Invoice-
to-Pay process. In a traditional organization, processing an invoice can involve many
manual activities. An employee may have to read the invoice, identify the vendor,
verify the purchase order, compare amounts, check for suspicious information,
decide whether approval is required, and finally process the payment. When these
tasks are performed manually for hundreds or thousands of invoices, they can
consume a significant amount of time and can also lead to human errors.
Through this project, I learned how such a repetitive workflow can be converted into
an intelligent, agent-driven system. Instead of asking one AI model to perform the
entire process, we divided the workflow into multiple specialized agents. Each agent
has a specific responsibility, such as extracting invoice information, validating the
invoice, checking risks, deciding the appropriate approval route, and executing the
final step.
The project also taught me an important principle of AI-based automation:
automation does not necessarily mean removing humans completely. In financial
processes, some decisions are too important to be left entirely to an automated
system. Therefore, Operon follows a Human-in-the-Loop approach in which low-risk
invoices can move through the workflow automatically, while high-risk or high-value
invoices can be sent to a human for approval.
Overall, the project helped me develop technical knowledge as well as problem-
solving, system-design, and analytical skills.

1. Understanding a Real-World Business Problem
One of the first and most important things I learned was how to identify a real-world
problem that can benefit from technology.

It is easy to build a software application around a technical idea, but building a useful
application requires understanding what problem the user actually faces. In the case
of Operon, the problem is the repetitive and time-consuming nature of invoice
processing.
An invoice may contain many different types of information, including vendor details,
invoice number, purchase order number, amount, due date, payment terms, bank
information, and line items. A finance employee may have to manually verify each of
these details before an invoice can be approved.
I learned that when designing an automation system, the first step should not be
choosing an AI model or programming language. The first step should be
understanding the workflow.
The Invoice-to-Pay process can be represented as:
Invoice Received
↓
Information Extraction
↓
Validation
↓
Risk Checking
↓
Approval Decision
↓
Payment
↓
Audit
By understanding this workflow, it became possible to identify which steps could be
automated and which steps should remain under human supervision.
This taught me an important software engineering principle: a good solution begins
with a clear understanding of the problem.

2. Learning How to Break a Complex Problem Into Smaller Components
Another major lesson from this project was decomposition.
Initially, invoice processing may look like one large task. However, when the process
is examined carefully, it consists of multiple smaller tasks.
For example:
 Extract information from the invoice.
 Check whether the vendor exists.

 Check whether the purchase order exists.
 Compare invoice and purchase order amounts.
 Identify suspicious patterns.
 Determine whether approval is required.
 Process the payment.
 Record what happened.
Instead of implementing all of these activities in one large function, the project
divides them into specialized agents.
The architecture consists of:
1. Intake Agent
2. Validation Agent
3. Risk Agent
4. Routing Agent
5. Execution Agent
This taught me that complex systems become easier to design and maintain when
they are divided into smaller modules with clearly defined responsibilities.
For example, the Intake Agent does not need to decide whether an invoice is risky.
Its job is primarily to understand the invoice and extract useful information. Similarly,
the Risk Agent does not need to perform every part of the invoice processing
workflow.
This separation of responsibilities makes the system easier to understand, test,
modify, and improve.

3. Understanding Multi-Agent AI Systems
One of the most important technical concepts I learned was the idea of a multi-agent
AI system.
Before this project, AI could be viewed simply as a model that receives an input and
produces an output. However, the project showed me that AI can be incorporated
into a larger workflow where multiple specialized components work together.
In Operon, the agents form a pipeline:
Intake Agent
↓
Validation Agent

↓
Risk Agent
↓
Routing Agent
↓
Execution Agent
Each agent contributes to a different part of the overall process.
The Intake Agent processes invoice information.
The Validation Agent checks whether the extracted information is consistent with
business records.
The Risk Agent looks for unusual or potentially problematic invoices.
The Routing Agent determines what should happen next.
The Execution Agent handles the final processing step after approval.
This taught me that the strength of an AI system does not necessarily come from
asking one model to do everything. A better approach can be to combine AI
capabilities with deterministic business logic and workflow management.

4. Learning About AI-Based Information Extraction
Another important learning was how AI can process unstructured information.
Invoices may not always follow exactly the same format. Different vendors can use
different layouts, descriptions, and structures. Extracting useful information from
such documents manually can be time-consuming.
Gemini AI is used in Operon to understand invoice information and extract structured
fields.
For example, an invoice may contain information such as:
Vendor: ABC Corporation
Invoice Number: INV-1025
Amount: $4,500
Currency: USD
PO Number: PO-2004
Due Date: 15 September
Instead of relying entirely on fixed positions or manually programmed rules, AI can
understand the content and produce structured information.
This taught me an important concept: AI is particularly useful when dealing with
unstructured or semi-structured information.

However, I also learned that AI output should not automatically be treated as perfect
or final. Extracted information should still be validated before it is used for an
important financial decision.

5. Understanding the Role of Gemini AI
Through this project, I also learned how an external AI API can be integrated into a
web application.
The project uses Google's Gemini AI through the @google/genai package.
The general process is:
Invoice Information
↓
Backend
↓
Gemini API
↓
AI Processing
↓
Structured Result
↓
Backend Workflow
This helped me understand that an AI model does not necessarily run independently
from the application. It can be integrated into the backend and become one
component of a larger software architecture.
I also learned the importance of designing a clear boundary between AI and normal
application logic.
AI is useful for tasks such as:
 Understanding text.
 Extracting information.
 Identifying pattern
