What you built and what you learnt:
Parista (Parikshya + Rista = "examine the relationship, before you react") is an agentic AI system that helps people navigate emotionally charged interpersonal conflicts breakups, family friction, workplace disputes with a manager or HR by grounding every piece of advice in real, cited psychological research instead of generic chatbot sympathy.

A user describes their situation, in text or as a screenshot of a chat conversation, through a Telegram bot or web app. That messy, unstructured input is passed through a six-agent pipeline built on Google ADK:

1. Safety check - screens every input for crisis signals before anything else runs.
2. Classification -tags the conflict's domain, type, and emotional tone.
3. Retrieval -matches the situation against a curated psychological research corpus (Supabase + pgvector), falling back to real-time Semantic Scholar search when confidence is low.
4. Reasoning -produces a structured analysis grounded in the retrieved source.
5. Citation verification -checks every claim traces back to a real, retrievable source before it reaches the user. This step fails closed: if a claim can't be verified, it is not shown, rather than risking an invented citation.
6. Style calibration -rewrites the grounded analysis into a natural, age-appropriate suggested reply, while keeping any follow-up questions consistent with the original grounded analysis.

How we built it

Backend is a modular FastAPI monolith orchestrating Google ADK agents, backed by Supabase (Postgres + pgvector) for both structured data and vector retrieval. Gemini handles the quality-sensitive reasoning and citation-verification steps, with a lighter model used for routine rephrasing to keep latency and cost down. Screenshot-based inputs go through vision-based OCR before entering the same pipeline as text. We used a spec-driven workflow (Spec Kit artifacts in the repo -spec, plan, tasks, data model, API contracts) to keep the multi-agent design consistent as we built, and we're testing with pytest for the backend and Playwright for end-to-end flows.

What we learnt

The hardest part wasn't the retrieval or the LLM reasoning -it was designing the citation-verification step to be strict enough to actually catch invented or misattributed claims without becoming so conservative that it refused to answer reasonable questions. We iterated on the boundary between "not enough evidence, refuse" and "enough evidence, ground and answer" several times. We also learned a lot about safety-check calibration -distinguishing real emotional distress (which is the whole premise of the product) from crisis-level signals that need a different, much more careful response path. Finally, working across Telegram, web, FastAPI, and ADK agents in parallel taught us a lot about keeping a multi-agent system's behavior consistent across different client interfaces.
Anything else for the judges: We chose Track C because Parista's core mechanism is a hard citation-verification gate that fails closed on unverifiable claims - the same grounded, non-hallucinating behavior the track asks for, just applied to conflict advice instead of policy documents. We'd encourage judges to test it with ambiguous inputs to see the refusal and fallback-retrieval behavior directly, not just the happy path.

What you built and what you learnt:
We built DevPilot AI, a developer productivity platform that takes a repository and does a whole bunch of things to it automatically. You upload a zip or paste a GitHub link, and the system analyzes the codebase, reviews the code with severity-graded findings, generates documentation and tests, lets you chat with the code, and gives you a health score across five dimensions. It's built as a FastAPI backend in Python with a React frontend in TypeScript, using Vite and Tailwind. The interesting part is the AI layer: we made seven agents, each responsible for one job, and each one talks to a different LLM provider — Groq for analysis and docs, Hugging Face for review, NVIDIA for tests, OpenRouter for chat and health, plus a pure rule-based security agent that never touches an LLM. Everything falls back to local rule-based logic if a provider key is missing, so the whole app works offline with a single mock key. Storage also degrades: MongoDB Atlas and Pinecone in production, SQLite and a local JSON index when you're just running it on a laptop.
Honestly, the hardest part was not the AI glue, it was making everything reliable and proving it. We spent a lot of time on CI/CD. The repo has four GitHub Actions workflows: one for the backend (lint plus 123 tests), one for the frontend (lint, typecheck, tests, production build), one for Playwright end-to-end tests, and one that builds Docker images on version tags. Getting all of those green was a grind. The end-to-end tests were the worst — they kept hanging for minutes before failing. The real cause turned out to be that the test file was written against an old version of the UI, targeting buttons and labels that no longer existed after a redesign. Every selector timed out. Once we rewrote the spec to match the actual interface — things like the fact that a segmented control exposes role "tab" instead of role "button" — the whole suite ran in about twenty seconds. That was a great lesson: when your UI changes, your tests change with it, and a hanging test is usually a stale selector, not a slow machine.
We also hit weird environment problems. Files that came over from another machine via WhatsApp carried macOS quarantine attributes, which blocked node binaries from running. Removing those attributes fixed the build. We ran into a fake dependency missing from the requirements file, and a dead-zone where the Python linter was complaining about a command-injection rule for a git call. Small, annoying, but each one taught us how these pipelines actually behave.
The other big piece of work was the documentation. We wrote a proper PRD describing what the system is, who it's for, and what it must do, with acceptance criteria per feature. We wrote a task breakdown that shows the progression phase by phase, with evidence for every item, because evaluators care about seeing how you got there, not just the final result. We added mermaid diagrams to the architecture doc and README so the system is visible at a glance — client, backend, orchestrator, agents, skills, providers, storage — and a couple of sequence diagrams for the main flows.
Code quality was another thread. The backend already used Ruff, and the frontend used ESLint plus TypeScript strict mode, so we didn't add new tools, we strengthened the existing ones. We enabled Ruff's own RUF rule family and cleaned out noqa comments that were dead — they referenced rules that weren't even in the active set anymore. One mistake: if you run ruff with --select RUF100 it overrides your whole config, so it flagged legitimate noqa directives as dead and removing them surfaced real security-rule violations. We caught it by running the full config afterward, reverted, and only removed the ones that were genuinely unused under the real settings. That taught us to always validate with the exact command CI runs, not a quick variant. We also turned on noUnusedLocals and noUnusedParameters in TypeScript, which passed clean because ESLint had already caught those.
What I actually learned: first, that a "production-shaped" demo is mostly about graceful failure. Everything in this app can break silently and still work — no provider key, no database, no vector store — and that's intentional and testable. Second, that agent architecture with a provider registry is a clean way to build AI features; adding or swapping a model is a config change, not a rewrite. Third, that CI is the source of truth. Local "it works on my machine" is a trap; the only thing that counts is whether the exact commands in the workflow pass in a clean environment. Fourth, that documentation is part of the deliverable. The PRD, the architecture doc, the task breakdown with real evidence, and the honest notes about what's still drifting are what make a project feel finished rather than demo-y.
At the end of the day we have a working product, a green pipeline, a tagged release, and a stack of docs that explain it. The biggest remaining gap is a real public deployment — the deploy workflow only builds images, it doesn't push them anywhere yet. That's the natural next step.
Anything else for the judges: DevPilot AI is an AI developer productivity platform: upload a repo (ZIP or GitHub), and it analyzes, reviews, documents, tests, and scores it via seven specialized agents, each routed to a different LLM provider with offline rule-based fallback. Built on FastAPI + React, with MongoDB/SQLite, Pinecone/local RAG, and a green CI/CD pipeline (123 backend tests, 5 frontend, Playwright E2E, ruff/eslint/tsc). Every workflow is explainable — findings carry file/line provenance. Docs, PRD, and task breakdown are in-repo. Key gap: public deployment not yet live.

What you built and what you learnt:
What We Built

Fairline is an agent-driven expense and reimbursement discrepancy resolution system. Employees submit expense claims with a receipt; a custom AI agent (Gemini 1.5 Flash Vision) extracts structured data from the receipt image; a custom deterministic policy engine checks that data against business rules (amount mismatch, missing documentation, low extraction confidence); clean claims are auto-approved instantly, and anything that trips a rule gets routed to a human approver with a clear "evidence packet" explaining exactly why. Every state change — submission, extraction, policy check, human decision — is written to an immutable audit log, so the entire lifecycle of a claim is traceable end to end.

The system is built on FastAPI + Firebase/Firestore on the backend, Next.js + Tailwind on the frontend, with Playwright end-to-end tests, Ruff/ESLint linting, and a GitHub Actions CI pipeline enforcing all of it on every push.

What We Learned

Human-in-the-loop is a design discipline, not a feature you bolt on. The hardest part wasn't getting an LLM to read a receipt — it was deciding exactly where automation should stop and a human should take over, and building the system so that boundary is enforced in code (the policy engine can never be bypassed, and every escalation path always requires a human's explicit decision), not just implied.

Agent-driven development still requires you to actually read the diff. Partway through the build, we switched coding tools mid-session and let it generate several iterations without reviewing each one closely — which is exactly the "blind, unreviewed auto-generation" pattern this kind of hackathon explicitly warns against. Catching that, going back through the commit history, and manually verifying the generated code against our own architecture doc and agent rules turned out to be as important as writing the original spec. It reinforced that the "human approving what matters" principle applies to how you build the system, not just what the system does at runtime.

Failure needs to be a first-class state, not an afterthought. Our extraction agent needs a live Gemini API key to function — and at one point in the build, that key was missing entirely. Instead of crashing, the system caught the failure, logged it to the audit trail as extraction_failed, and continued the claim through the policy engine with default values rather than blocking the whole pipeline. That wasn't originally planned as a design decision so much as it emerged from testing edge cases — but it turned out to be one of the more valuable things in the system, because it means a real-world API outage doesn't take down the whole triage process.

Infrastructure surprises eat real time. We lost close to an hour to a GitHub Actions runner allocation failure that had nothing to do with our code — a good reminder that "green CI" as a gating requirement means you need buffer time for things entirely outside your control, not just your own bugs.
Anything else for the judges:
A Note for the Judges

Where we cut scope, deliberately:
This was built on a compressed timeline (docs finalized overnight, full build in a single day). We made conscious cuts to protect the core loop rather than spread thin: no auth (view toggles instead), only 3 hardcoded policy rules instead of a dynamic rule engine, single-page image uploads only. Everything we cut is documented explicitly in our PRD's "Out of Scope" section — we'd rather show a judge a small thing that fully works than a large thing that half-works.

Where the system is honest about its own limits:
If the Gemini extraction call fails for any reason (bad key, API outage, malformed image), the system doesn't silently guess or crash — it logs extraction_failed to the audit trail and routes the claim forward with default values rather than blocking the pipeline. We think a production-facing agent system should degrade visibly, not silently.

On our process:
We used BMAD's Analyst → PM → Architect planning methodology (run manually via chat to conserve API quota, per the hackathon's own rate-limit guidance) before writing any code, and Cline as our coding agent throughout, wired to our own free-tier API keys. Partway through the build we caught ourselves letting a session run unreviewed, and treated that as a genuine process failure worth fixing rather than ignoring — we went back through the commit history and manually verified everything against our own architecture doc before continuing. We think that's a more honest account of agent-driven development than pretending every step was perfectly supervised from minute one.

What we'd build next, given more time:
Duplicate-claim detection, a dynamic rule-builder UI for finance admins, and extending the same evidence-packet pattern to categories beyond expenses (HR grievances, academic integrity cases) — the underlying architecture (extract → validate → escalate → audit) was designed to generalize beyond finance, we just scoped this build to one workflow to build it properly rather than three shallowly.

What you built and what you learnt:
PMX began as a Go port of Picomatch for Port Mortem (LINK FOR VIEWING THE PICOMATCH-GO RUNTIME:-https://github.com/debayansamal/port-mortem-picomatch-go). During the project, we expanded the port into a developer and agent validation system while keeping the Picomatch runtime itself isolated and testable.
The resulting system has three major layers:
1. Picomatch-compatible Go runtime
The core runtime implements the Picomatch matching pipeline:
Scan → Parse → Compile → Match
with support for globstars, braces, negation, dotfiles, POSIX character classes, Windows path behavior and compatibility/regression coverage.
2. PMX CLI
The runtime is exposed through a developer-facing CLI with commands including:
match, scan, parse, explain, validate, compat, doctor, agent, ci, fuzz, and bench.
We then built a structured diagnostics layer around the CLI. pmx doctor --json produces machine-readable project diagnostics, while pmx doctor --ci provides automation-oriented pass/warn/fail semantics.
The first concrete ecosystem adapter is JavaScript/TypeScript project diagnostics, including package-manager/lockfile detection, TypeScript configuration, ESLint configuration and actionable diagnostic codes.
3. Agent-driven lifecycle validation
The most important evolution was making PMX usable by coding agents rather than only humans.
pmx agent inspect --json provides an agent-readable project snapshot.
pmx agent check --json is the canonical ADLC gate and emits a stable machine-readable contract:
version, result, diagnostics, checks, and next_actions.
The intended lifecycle is:
INSPECT → DIAGNOSE → FIX → CHECK → REGRESSION → CI → REPORT
We also committed a custom PMX validation agent and custom PMX Doctor/ADLC skill so an agent can follow a bounded verification workflow instead of relying on ad-hoc prompts.
4. Engineering Foundry
We built a Next.js dashboard intended to act as the control plane for PMX.
The important design principle is that Foundry should display real execution evidence, not simulated status. Its validation API executes the PMX CLI, captures exit codes, stdout/stderr, duration and structured JSON, and exposes those results to the UI.
The same principle applies to GitHub Actions: workflow state, jobs, logs and artifacts are obtained from the GitHub API rather than fabricated by the dashboard.
We also created a repository CI pipeline covering formatting, linting, vetting, unit tests, race tests, builds, CLI checks, doctor, ADLC checks, compatibility, regression, fuzzing, benchmarks and dashboard validation.
What we learnt
The biggest lesson was that porting a runtime is only one part of building a useful developer tool. The more interesting problem became proving that software is actually healthy.
That led us to a central architectural principle:
one execution engine, one structured evidence contract, multiple consumers.
Developers, coding agents, CI and Foundry should consume the same validation evidence instead of maintaining separate implementations of project health.
PMX therefore evolved from a language-porting project into an experiment in agent-driven software lifecycle validation: a developer can run PMX manually, while an agent can inspect a repository, diagnose it, make changes, run the lifecycle gate and produce structured evidence that CI and other systems can consume.
Anything else for the judges:
PMX was deliberately built around reproducibility and evidence.
The repository contains the required architecture documentation, engineering/agent rules, custom agent, custom skill, and GitHub Actions workflow.
The important demo path is not a collection of static dashboard screens. The intended demonstration is:
Developer / Agent
       │
       ▼
pmx agent inspect --json
       │
       ▼
Diagnose
       │
       ▼
Fix project
       │
       ▼
pmx agent check --json
       │
       ▼
pmx ci --json
       │
       ├──────────────► Local evidence
       │
       ▼
GitHub Actions
       │
       ▼
Foundry
       │
       ├── workflow
       ├── jobs
       ├── logs
       └── artifacts
The Foundry validation panel can execute the PMX CLI directly, while the GitHub integration exposes the actual Actions state. This distinction is intentional: local validation is not presented as GitHub CI, and unavailable remote state is never converted into a fabricated PASS.
The project also includes deterministic JavaScript/TypeScript fixtures so diagnostic behavior can be regression-tested rather than demonstrated only against the developer's current machine.
Our remaining work is primarily hardening and verification: ensuring every CI job remains green, removing tooling/configuration incompatibilities, and ensuring every dashboard route visibly reflects its real execution result. The architecture itself is intentionally frozen rather than expanded into additional ecosystems before the core workflow is reliable.




The submitted demo video was recorded during the Port Mortem implementation window and demonstrates the core PMX runtime and CLI workflow.
After recording, we continued hardening the project around the submission requirements, particularly the GitHub Actions pipeline, ADLC contract, Foundry execution layer and CI validation surface.
During the final verification period, CI workflow regressions took longer than expected to resolve. In particular, the GitHub Actions lint environment exposed version/configuration incompatibilities in the golangci-lint configuration, which required workflow/toolchain fixes. Because those regressions were being resolved late in the submission window, I was not able to record a clean final walkthrough of the complete Foundry → GitHub Actions → jobs → logs → artifacts flow.
The dashboard execution path itself was implemented around real PMX command execution rather than static PASS states, and the repository contains the corresponding API routes, validation contracts and workflow integration.
I am intentionally calling out this limitation rather than presenting an unverified dashboard flow as working evidence.
The final product direction is:
Developer / Agent → PMX → structured evidence → CI → Foundry
with the same validation contract consumed throughout the lifecycle.
The project prioritizes reproducibility, agent usability and executable verification over adding more UI or unsupported ecosystem features.

What you built and what you learnt:
Project CCA: The Compliance and Compatibility Auditor
A Deep Dive Retrospective: Building an Automated Governance Engine in 48 Hours
Executive Summary
Modern software development operates at a breakneck pace. With the advent of microservices, continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, and distributed teams, code is merged and deployed dozens—sometimes hundreds—of times a day. While this agility drives innovation, it introduces a massive bottleneck: Governance.
Ensuring that every line of code, every third-party dependency, and every infrastructure-as-code (IaC) template complies with stringent legal frameworks (GDPR, HIPAA, SOC2) and internal compatibility matrices is a monumental task. Manual audits are too slow; traditional static analyzers are too narrow.
Enter Project CCA (Compliance and Compatibility Auditor).
Developed over a grueling 48-hour enterprise hackathon, Project CCA is an AI-augmented, event-driven engine designed to sit directly within the CI/CD pipeline. It intercepts pull requests, builds a dependency graph, cross-references internal compatibility matrices, and evaluates infrastructure against compliance policies using the Open Policy Agent (OPA).
This document serves as a comprehensive post-mortem and technical whitepaper detailing the genesis, architecture, implementation, and future roadmap of Project CCA.
1. The Problem Statement
Before diving into the solution, it is crucial to understand the exact friction points that led our hackathon team to tackle this specific challenge.
The Compliance Bottleneck
In highly regulated industries, software cannot simply "work"; it must be proven secure and compliant. When a developer adds a new logging library, they might inadvertently capture Personally Identifiable Information (PII). If this code reaches production, it violates GDPR, risking massive fines. Traditionally, security and compliance teams run quarterly audits or rely on heavy, post-merge scanning tools that take hours to run. This creates a "shift-right" problem, where issues are found too late in the software development lifecycle (SDLC), causing expensive rollbacks and delayed releases.
The Compatibility Nightmare
In a microservices architecture, Service A relies on Service B, which relies on a specific version of a shared library. When Service B updates that shared library, it might introduce breaking changes to the API that Service A consumes. We call this the "Compatibility Matrix Paradox." Dependency hell is a well-known issue, but in enterprise environments, it extends beyond package managers (like npm or pip) into service-level agreements and API contract testing.
The Hackathon Objective
Our goal was to build a system that achieves "Shift-Left Governance." We needed a tool that could:
Instantly analyze code changes at the Pull Request (PR) level.
Flag compliance violations (e.g., exposed ports, unencrypted databases, PII logging).
Check compatibility against a live matrix of active microservices.
Block the merge automatically if critical thresholds were breached, while providing actionable remediation advice to the developer.
2. Hackathon Context and Ideation
The hackathon kicked off on a Friday evening. The theme was "Frictionless Enterprise." Teams were tasked with building tools that removed roadblocks for internal engineering teams without sacrificing security.
Our team, consisting of two backend engineers, one DevOps specialist, and one frontend developer, congregated in a corner of the office. We started by mapping out the pain points we faced daily. The consensus was unanimous: waiting for the internal Security and Compliance board to approve infrastructure changes was the biggest velocity killer.
